strengths: The core idea—training the student to map (prompt, its own initial answer, teacher critique) to a teacher-refined answer—is a sensible and clearly motivated extension of Critique Fine-Tuning (CFT) that directly targets the format-drift problem, and the qualitative examples in Appendix A concretely illustrate the claimed behavioral difference.

Evaluation breadth is respectable: two training datasets (WebInstruct, MetaMathQA), eight reasoning/knowledge benchmarks, plus general-capability checks (IFEval, MUSR, TruthfulQA, BBH), and the IFEval degradation of CFT (76.6→55.6) vs. its preservation under CGD is a useful and practically relevant finding.

Several controlled comparisons strengthen the empirical case: a Distilled SFT baseline that shares the same teacher refinements, an ablation removing the critique from the input (Fig. 5), and a learning-rate sensitivity study (Table 4) showing CGD is more robust than CFT to hyperparameter choice.

All methods are trained on the same 100K samples with the same teacher and identical schedules, and the limitations section honestly acknowledges dependence on critique quality, dataset coverage, and critique bias.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution, presented as a central claim ('provably reduces output uncertainty'), is not sound. Lemma 1 is stated between ill-defined objects (KL between a marginal P(X) and a conditional Q(Y|Z), with the proof silently switching between P and R and between x and y), and conditioning on additional variables does not in general reduce KL divergence to a fixed target—Eq. (9) therefore does not follow. The 'Bayesian interpretation' in Eq. (10) asserts a posterior factorization that is never derived from the actual training objective, which is plain MLE on teacher targets. The abstract also claims an entropy-based empirical analysis, but no empirical entropy measurements appear anywhere in the paper.

The inference-time procedure is never specified, which is a serious train–test soundness gap. At training time the critique c comes from the teacher, but at deployment there is no teacher; the paper does not explain whether the student must self-generate a critique before answering (which contradicts the claims of single-pass inference and 'no additional inference-time cost' and introduces a distribution mismatch between teacher and student critiques), or how (x, y', c) inputs are constructed at test time. This omission makes the headline efficiency claim unverifiable.

Statistical rigor is insufficient for the magnitude of the headline claims. AMC23 has only 40 problems, so the celebrated +15–17.5% corresponds to roughly 6 questions, with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests on any benchmark. On the MetaMathQA setting (Table 3), CGD's advantage over CFT shrinks to +0.1–1.5 average and CGD actually loses on Minerva-Math, GSM8K, GPQA, and MMLU-Pro, so gains are far from uniform.

Baseline descriptions are inconsistent and confusing: Fig. 3's caption says CFT uses GPT-4o-generated critiques, while Table 1 presents a separate 'CFT*' GPT-4o variant and a LLaMA-teacher CFT; moreover GPT-4o-based CFT beats CGD on TheoremQA and MMLU-Pro, which complicates the 'consistently best' narrative.

Generality is limited to a single student (Llama3.1-8B) and a single teacher (Llama3.3-70B); the paper itself notes CFT's behavior is highly model-dependent (e.g., Qwen-2.5), yet no second model pair is tested to show CGD's advantages transfer.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or data release is mentioned, the critique/refinement prompts are not provided, decoding parameters and evaluation harness details are absent, and there are writing/citation sloppinesses (e.g., 'recent works has moved', 'basedline', duplicated references [6]/[7]) that suggest the manuscript needed another careful pass.

strengths: The core empirical idea is sensible and well-motivated: training the student to map (prompt, its own initial answer, teacher critique) to a refined answer is a natural way to internalize critique-and-revise behavior at no inference cost, and it addresses a real, documented failure mode of Critique Fine-Tuning (format drift).

The evaluation is reasonably broad for an 8B student: eight math/reasoning benchmarks plus IFEval, MUSR, TruthfulQA, and BBH, across two training sets (WebInstruct and MetaMathQA), with sensible baselines including Distilled SFT and a GPT-4o-teacher CFT variant that isolates teacher-quality confounds.

The ablations are useful: the with/without-critique ablation (Fig. 5) directly supports the central design choice, the learning-rate sensitivity study (Table 4) shows CGD is more stable than CFT, and the appendix provides concrete training-data and qualitative format-drift examples.

The paper is candid about the mixed MetaMathQA results (Table 3, where CGD loses to CFT on several tasks) and includes an honest limitations section discussing data-generation overhead and dependence on critique quality.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis, presented as one of three main contributions, is mathematically unsound. Lemma 1 compares KL(P(X)||Q(Y|Z)) to KL(P(X)||Q(Y|Z,C)), i.e., KL divergences between distributions over different random variables, which is ill-defined; the proof manipulates notation (R(X) versus Q(y|z)) in a way that does not establish any valid inequality, and the claimed guarantee that 'conditioning reduces KL' does not hold in general. Equation (9) therefore does not follow, and the 'provably reduces uncertainty' claim in the abstract and conclusion is unsupported.

The Bayesian interpretation (Eq. 10) is asserted, not derived: the proportionality S_θ(ŷ|x,y',c) ∝ T_φ(c|x,y',ŷ)·S_init(ŷ|x,y') is stated without justification, and the claim that Algorithm 1 (plain maximum likelihood on (x, y', c) → ŷ) 'directly implements' a KL minimization between a student posterior and a teacher-defined target is simply not true of the actual training objective.

The abstract claims 'Using entropy-based analysis, we show that CGD reduces refinement uncertainty,' but no entropy measurements appear anywhere in the paper—only the (trivial) conditional-entropy inequality, which does not by itself support the claim.

The headline numbers rest on extremely small, single-run evaluations with no variance or significance testing. AMC23 has 40 problems, so the celebrated +17.5% corresponds to 7 problems, and every result comes from one seed of one student/teacher pair (Llama3.1-8B → Llama3.3-70B); no other student families (e.g., Qwen, discussed in Sec. 4.3) are actually tested, so generality claims are weak.

There are numerical inconsistencies between text and tables: Section 4.3 claims CGD beats the strongest Group-2 baseline by '+4.8%', but Table 1's reported delta is +4.3%; the abstract reports '+15.0% over CFT' on AMC23 while the intro says '+17.5% and +15.0% absolute gains over SFT and CFT respectively' in a way that is easy to misread.

The training setup as described is difficult to believe and to reproduce: fine-tuning an 8B model on 100K samples in '30 minutes' on 16 A100s (8 GPU-hours) implies implausibly high throughput for long-form critique-augmented data, and no code, prompts for critique/refinement generation, decoding parameters, or evaluation harness details are provided or promised for release.

The IFEval 'catastrophic forgetting' analysis compares CFT* (GPT-4o critiques, 50K samples) against CGD (Llama teacher, 100K samples), conflating teacher quality and data scale with the training objective; the like-for-like CFT row is missing from Table 2.

Novelty is modest: the pipeline closely resembles prior critique-and-refine distillation work (Shridhar et al., Yu et al.), with the main delta being conditioning the student on the critique—so the paper leans heavily on the theoretical framing, which as noted does not hold.

Writing quality is below venue standard in places ('recent works has moved', 'we also CFT', 'strongest basedline', 'over which with to perform MLE'), and the Jensen's-inequality step in the Lemma 1 proof is presented with reversed/confusing inequality directions.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and practical: conditioning the student on its own initial answer plus a teacher critique and training it to produce the refined answer avoids the format drift observed in Critique Fine-Tuning (CFT), and the qualitative example in Appendix A.2 illustrates this concretely.

The empirical evaluation is broad: two training corpora (WebInstruct, MetaMathQA), two benchmark groups, four general-capability benchmarks (Table 2), a learning-rate robustness study (Table 4), and an input-ablation isolating the critique's contribution (Fig. 5). Consistent improvements over SFT, Distilled SFT, and CFT on the harder math benchmarks (OlympiadBench, AMC23) are encouraging.

The paper is transparent about training setup (teacher/student models, 100K samples, compute budget) and includes an honest limitations section discussing critique-quality dependence and computational overhead.
Related work is reasonably comprehensive, covering self-correction, feedback granularity, tool-augmented refinement, and pedagogical feedback, and the paper is well positioned relative to CFT [37].
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is unsound. Lemma 1 compares KL(P(X) || Q(Y|Z)) with KL(P(X) || Q(Y|Z,C)) — KL divergences between distributions over different variables/conditioning sets, which is not a well-defined comparison, and the claimed monotone reduction of KL to a fixed target by adding conditioning variables is generally false (conditional *entropy* decreases in expectation; KL to an arbitrary target does not). Eq. (9) inherits this problem: KL(P_D(y|x) || S_θ(y|x)) and KL(P_D(y|x) || S_θ(ŷ|x,y',c)) are over different supports, so the '≥' claim that CGD 'provably reduces output uncertainty' and 'starts from a better optimization point' is not actually established. The proof's notation (mixing R(x), P(X), summing over x with y treated as fixed) is also sloppy.

The Bayesian interpretation (Eq. 10) is asserted, not derived: nothing in the MLE objective (Eq. 1) forces the learned student to factor as teacher-likelihood times student prior, and T_φ(c|x,y',ŷ) is never validated as a likelihood. This framing is decorative rather than substantive.

The inference-time protocol is unclear and undercuts a central claim. Training conditions on (x, y', c), but the paper claims single-pass inference with no extra cost. If at test time the model receives only x, there is a train–test input mismatch that is never discussed; if the model first generates its own answer and critique, that is a multi-pass procedure contradicting the 'no inference overhead' claim. This must be specified precisely.

The comparison to Distilled SFT is potentially confounded: the description suggests Distilled SFT also uses teacher refinements generated from (x, y', c). If its training input differs from CGD's only by the critique, then the headline gains largely reduce to the input-ablation in Fig. 5, and the framing as a new learning 'paradigm' overstates the delta over existing refinement-distillation work (e.g., Shridhar et al. [30], Yu et al. [44]).

Statistical rigor is weak. AMC23 has ~40 problems, so the headline +15–17.5% jumps correspond to a handful of items; no standard deviations, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, and several GSM8K/Minerva-Math results are within noise. Reported numbers are also internally inconsistent: the abstract/intro claim +17.5% over SFT and +15.0% over CFT on AMC23, but Table 1 shows +15.0% over both.

Teacher-quality confound: CFT with a GPT-4o teacher (CFT*) beats CGD on several Group 1 tasks, and the paper acknowledges CFT gains depend on teacher quality, yet CGD is never tested with a stronger teacher, leaving the claim that CGD is the better use of critique signals incompletely supported.

Reproducibility gaps: no code or data release mentioned, the critique-generation and refinement prompts (arguably the crux of the method) are not provided, and hyperparameters/decoding settings for evaluation are sparse. Also, '16 A100 GPUs for 30 minutes' for fine-tuning an 8B model on 100K examples (8 GPU-hours) is implausibly low and suggests either an error or that the data was seen for far less than one epoch — either way this needs clarification.

Presentation quality is below bar for a main-track submission: numerous grammatical errors ('often suffer', 'recent works has moved', 'strongest basedline'), inconsistent claims between abstract and tables, and an appendix dominated by long verbatim generation dumps.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated training recipe: conditioning the student on (prompt, its own initial answer, teacher critique) while targeting the refined answer is a natural fix for CFT's format-drift problem, and the single-pass inference design means zero inference overhead — a practically valuable property.

Comprehensive experimental coverage: two student-teacher pairs (LLaMA and S1.1 families), two training datasets, additional student architectures (Mixtral, OLMo), teacher ablations (Table 8), learning-rate sensitivity (Table 4), critique-correctness mixture ablation (Fig. 5), and general-capability benchmarks (Table 2) showing CGD preserves instruction-following while CFT degrades IFEval by ~21 points.

The key ablation isolating the critique as a learning signal (Fig. 4) is informative, and the finding that a balanced mixture of correct/incorrect examples (Fig. 5) is optimal is a useful practical insight.
The paper is generally well-written with a clear method description (Algorithm 1), an honest limitations section, and supplied code/configurations that aid reproducibility.
Hyperparameter robustness comparison (Table 4) and training-loss analysis (Fig. 8) support the claim that CGD is more stable than CFT.
weaknesses: Inconsistency in the RL comparison (Table 3): the CGD numbers there (e.g., MATH500 = 29.4) differ drastically from Table 1 (54.2), and it is unclear whether CGD was applied to the base model rather than the Instruct model described throughout the paper. This inconsistency, in the headline '60x less compute' claim, undermines that comparison. The claimed compute advantage also excludes the substantial teacher-inference cost of generating 100K critiques and refinements.

No statistical treatment in the main results despite claims of 3-seed averaging: AMC23 has only 40 problems, so the headline +15.0% gain corresponds to ~6 questions, yet no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for Tables 1, 6, 7, 8. Some per-benchmark gains (e.g., MMLU-PRO -0.2 on S1.1, GPQA -1.1 on OLMo) suggest noise-level effects.

The diagnostic analyses are weak evidence for the mechanistic claims. Single-next-token Shannon entropy differences of 6.44 vs 6.49 (Table 9) are tiny despite the p-value, the gradient-norm reduction with critique conditioning (Table 10) is trivially expected since conditioning on more information lowers loss, and the attention 'plan-then-execute' narrative (Figs. 9-11) is post-hoc descriptive over only 50 samples. The Bayesian interpretation (Eq. 2) is informal: the paper claims CGD 'minimizes KL divergence' between posteriors, but the actual objective is plain NLL on teacher outputs.

Novelty is modest: distilling refined answers conditioned on the student's own output and teacher feedback closely resembles prior refine-tuning/self-correction distillation work (e.g., Yu et al., 2024b; Shridhar et al., 2023), differing mainly in moving critique-conditioning into the training input. The 'internalizes why' framing is asserted more than demonstrated — at test time the model receives neither its initial answer nor a critique, so the learned skill is not self-correction in the usual sense.

Baseline results raise questions: vanilla SFT substantially degrades the base model on most math benchmarks (e.g., LLaMA 41.2 vs 50.6 on MATH500), which is atypical and suggests tuning or data-format issues that are not analyzed; likewise GSM8K losses after SFT go unexplained.

Mixtral/OLMo and MetaMathQA ablations show mixed or small gains (e.g., Group 1 delta of only 1.5 for OLMo, and +1.5 for MetaMathQA), tempering the 'consistent, robust across families' claim made in the abstract and intro.

strengths: The core idea — conditioning the student on (prompt, its own initial answer, teacher critique) during training while keeping inference single-pass and prompt-only — is simple, practical, and distinct from CFT, and it plausibly avoids the format-drift failure mode documented for CFT.

Broad empirical coverage: two student–teacher pairs (LLaMA and S1.1), two training datasets (WebInstruct, MetaMathQA), additional student architectures (Mixtral, OLMo), teacher-model ablations, critique-composition ablations, learning-rate sensitivity, epoch curves, and preservation of general capabilities (IFEval, MUSR, TruthfulQA, BBH) where CFT degrades sharply (76.6% to 55.6% on IFEval).

Useful ablation isolating the critique as a training signal (Figure 4): performance drops substantially when the critique is removed from training inputs even though it is absent at inference, which is the paper's most interesting empirical finding.
Reasonable reproducibility support: hyperparameter table (Table 5), an example training sample (Appendix D), and a code archive with evaluation pipelines and LLaMA-Factory configs.
The paper includes an explicit limitations section and honestly reports settings where CGD underperforms (e.g., OLMo gains are small, AMC23 regression for Mixtral, CFT* with GPT-4o competitive).
weaknesses: Train–test mismatch is under-theorized. At inference the model sees neither its own initial answer nor the critique, yet the central narrative (Bayesian posterior update, Eq. 2; 'learning the posterior P(y|x,c)') only describes the with-critique setting. The paper never explains why training-time conditioning transfers to prompt-only inference, which is the actual mechanism behind the headline gains. The Bayesian framing is decorative and does not support the claims.

The RL comparison (Table 3) is confounded: SimpleRL-Zero trains the LLaMA3.1-8B base model, while CGD starts from the instruction-tuned LLaMA3.1-8B Instruct. Claiming 'approaches or exceeds SimpleRL-Zero with 60x less compute' is not an apples-to-apples compute or capability comparison, and SimpleRL actually wins on AMC23 (15.0 vs 10.0) and ties on AIME24 (0.0 for both).

Internally inconsistent resource reporting: Section 4.1.2 states all experiments use 16 A100s for 30 minutes (8 GPU-hours), while Section 4.2.1 claims 8 A100s for ~5 hours (~40 GPU-hours). The abstract's '60x less compute' claim rests on numbers the paper itself contradicts.

No variance or significance reporting for the main results despite claiming means over three random seeds (A.1). Several headline gains are within evaluation noise, especially on small benchmarks (AMC23 has 40 problems, so all reported values are multiples of 2.5 and a '+15.0' gain is 6 problems).

Arithmetic/reporting errors undermine confidence: the introduction claims '+12.9% over SFT' on OlympiadBench for LLaMA3.1-8B, but Table 1 gives 23.7 vs 14.5 (+9.2); abstract advertises 'Qwen family' results while footnote 3 concedes Qwen could not be used (S1.1 is used instead).

Mechanistic analyses are over-interpreted. A 0.05-nat mean-entropy difference (6.44 vs 6.49) is elevated to the model being 'a uniquely robust and decisive reasoning agent'; the 27% lower gradient norm is expected whenever conditioning reduces loss and is not evidence of 'more efficient learning'; attention-flow observations are described with causal language ('plan-then-execute') that the analysis cannot establish. The counterfactual robustness claim rests on a single sample (#42).

Related work positioning understates overlap: prior critique-and-refine fine-tuning (Shridhar et al. 2023; Yu et al. 2024b) already trains on student initial outputs plus teacher feedback; the delta is mainly that the critique is dropped at inference, which is closer to auxiliary-conditioned distillation than a new training paradigm.
Contamination is not discussed: training on MetaMathQA (derived from MATH/GSM8K) and evaluating on MATH500/GSM8K raises leakage concerns that are unexamined.

Fairness of the central CFT comparison depends on the teacher: CFT* with GPT-4o nearly matches CGD on LLaMA (36.4 vs 36.7 average) and beats it on TheoremQA and MMLU-PRO, so the 'state-of-the-art' claim is teacher-dependent and softer than presented.

strengths: The core idea is simple, sensible, and clearly motivated: conditioning the student on (prompt, its own initial answer, teacher critique) while training it to emit the teacher's refined answer addresses the documented format-drift failure of CFT and, unlike prior self-correction fine-tuning, requires no critique at inference time.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this line of work: two student-teacher families, four student architectures (LLaMA, S1.1, Mixtral, OLMo), two training datasets, multiple teachers, learning-rate sensitivity, critique-correctness mixture ablation, and epoch-accuracy curves, with code and a training-data example provided for reproducibility.

The paper is honest that gains vary (e.g., negative deltas on GPQA/AMC23 for Mixtral and Minerva-Math/GSM8K on MetaMathQA in Appendix B.1) and includes a genuine limitations section acknowledging student receptivity and data-generation cost.

The fair Distilled SFT baseline (same teacher refinements, same data) makes the critique-as-conditioning-signal comparison meaningful, and the ablation 'CGD without critique' isolates the critique's contribution.
Preserving general capabilities (IFEval, MUSR, TruthfulQA, BBH) while improving math reasoning is a practically valuable property relative to CFT's -21% IFEval degradation.
weaknesses: The central train-test mismatch is under-analyzed: the model is trained conditioned on its own initial answer and a critique, but at inference sees only the prompt. The paper asserts this teaches the student to 'internalize the critique,' but never tests the natural alternatives (e.g., conditioning at test time on the student's own generated answer and critique, or an input-noising curriculum), leaving the mechanism speculative and the design choice unvalidated against the most obvious deployment-matched variant.

Several headline gains rest on very small test sets without variance reporting: AMC23 has 40 problems, so the advertised +15.0% is 6 problems; no confidence intervals or significance tests accompany the main tables (seeds are averaged but not reported). The abstract's bold numbers therefore overstate statistical certainty.

The abstract's '+17.5% over SFT on AMC23' is inflated because vanilla SFT substantially degrades LLaMA3.1-8B (e.g., MATH500 50.6 to 41.2); gains relative to a harmful baseline are not evidence of the method's absolute value.

Diagnostic claims are over-interpreted: the entropy difference (6.44 vs. 6.49 for Distilled SFT) is minuscule in effect size despite p < 10^-4, yet the paper concludes CGD 'forges a uniquely robust and decisive reasoning agent.' The counterfactual robustness claim rests on a single case study (Sample #42), which is anecdotal and presented in a way that suggests generality.

The 'Bayesian interpretation' (Sec. 3.2, App. C.5) is hand-wavy: the KL minimization described is just standard SFT cross-entropy on the conditioned target; the posterior framing adds little and the claimed teacher 'likelihood' is not estimated.

Novelty is incremental relative to CFT (Wang et al., 2025) and prior critique-then-refine distillation (Shridhar et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2024b); the contribution is a conditioning/target swap rather than a new framework, so the repeated 'novel' and 'state-of-the-art' framing overstates the advance.

The abstract claims gains 'across LLaMA and Qwen families,' but no Qwen models are directly used; S1.1 is a Qwen-derived fine-tune and the paper itself notes (footnote 3) it could not use Qwen models, so the claim is loose. The '60x less compute' figure also appears only in the abstract while the body says 'well over an order of magnitude,' an inconsistency that should be reconciled.

Missing important baselines such as RFT/verifier-filtered SFT and a comparison where the same teacher-refinement budget is spent without critiques, to confirm the critique pipeline (not just teacher refinement) drives the gains.
